verdict_reason: The new equal-time comparison can still discard a blocking weekly window because it prioritizes primary usage over secondary usage.
reply_markdown:
1. **Yes—finding #1.** At the same observation time, A=(primary 30%, secondary 99%) loses to B=(primary 31%, secondary 10%) in either recorded order. With future resets, A blocks and B does not. The same issue affects live replacement. Contrary to the handoff, `newer_wins` compares `max(primary, secondary)`; the new helper compares a lexicographic tuple. A blocking observation selected from sub-agents can therefore lose during endpoint selection.

   The original primary-only F46-1 example is fixed, but its broader blocking-window invariant remains incomplete. Both inspected tests omit competing secondary windows.

2. **HOLD; do not tag v0.2.1 yet.** Resolve finding #1 and run RC1. Two existing test-executable cases passed: the new recorded primary tie test and the existing `newer_wins` test. These were prebuilt binaries; their exact source revision was not established. No files were written.

Reading covered all three non-`.collab` changed paths and targeted aggregation/health context. `.collab` changes were skipped as instructed, apart from handoffs 47 and 45. The broader wave-8 implementation, external plugin sources/harnesses, and unrelated prior findings were not re-reviewed. Checkout HEAD was `e4690dc`, beyond the requested endpoint; the changed hunks were read from the explicit range.

## Requested checks

- **RC1:** From repository root, with **workspace-write** permission, add equal-time fixtures A=(30,99), B=(31,10), both resets future; exercise both recorded orders, both recorded/live assignments, and sub-agent aggregation feeding endpoint selection. Run `cargo test -p c3-core quota -j 2`. Every path must preserve weekly blocking. Budget: 30 minutes.

findings.claim: The replacement equal-time rule can hide a blocking secondary window: lexicographic comparison prioritizes any higher primary percentage over a 99% secondary percentage. It also differs from the existing rollout/sub-agent rule, which compares the maximum usage across both windows. Consequently, an endpoint can remain available despite an equally recent blocking weekly observation.
findings.trigger: For the same endpoint and observed_at, observation A has primary=30 and secondary=99, while B has primary=31 and secondary=10; all reset times are in the future. Recorded selection chooses B in either order. Recorded B also rejects live A, and live B replaces recorded A.

evidence.observation: window_obs_wins compares (primary used_percent, secondary used_percent) with tuple > and is used by both recorded selection and live replacement.
Observation::fullest returns max(primary, secondary); newer_wins uses that value for equal timestamps in sub-agent and account-rollout selection.
Either window blocks at usage >=98 with a future reset, but health evaluates only the observation retained by endpoint_window.
The tuple comparison always selects B, which has no blocking window, although A has a blocking weekly window.

evidence.reference: target/debug/deps/c3_core-a4af68ba455879d7.exe: exact recorded-tie and newer_wins unit tests
evidence.observation: Both tests passed. Their inspected fixtures do not test competing secondary usage, so these passes do not establish the requested invariant; binary revision was not verified.

findings.verification: Run RC1 with both input orders and both recorded/live assignments; require the resulting endpoint quota to retain the 99% weekly block.
findings.remedy: Use one consistent equal-time selection policy across recorded, live, and sub-agent aggregation that preserves the blocking secondary observation; align the endpoint helper with the existing fullest-window rule for this case and add cross-window regression tests. Correct the documentation's assertion that the current rules are equivalent.
